case_info.scenario: A 43-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of recurring symptoms of sudden onset of fatigue, palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, lightheadedness, and nausea that were associated with standing and resolved with sitting. These symptoms began 1 month after mild COVID-19 infection. At presentation, while supine, blood pressure (BP) was 123/70 mm Hg and heart rate (HR) was 90/min; while seated, BP was 120/80 and HR was 93/min; after standing for 1 minute, BP was 124/80 and HR was 119/min. Physical examination results were normal. Oxygen saturation was 98% at rest while breathing room air. She had no oxygen desaturation during a 6-minute walk test but walked only 282 m (45% predicted). Complete blood cell count, morning cortisol, and thyrotropin blood levels were normal. Electrocardiogram (ECG), chest computed tomography, pulmonary function testing, methacholine challenge, bronchoscopy, echocardiography, and cardiac catheterization findings were normal. During tilt table testing, the patient experienced lightheadedness and nausea when moved from horizontal to the upright position. Results of the tilt table test are shown in theTableandFigure.
case_info.explanation: D. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) Tilt table testing is performed in the inpatient or outpatient setting and measures an individual’s symptoms and hemodynamic response to the downward displacement of intravascular volume with movement from the supine to upright position. During tilt table testing, movement from horizontal to upright positioning normally provokes an increase in sympathetic adrenergic outflow to sustain cardiac output. A normal response is a mild decrease in BP (decline in systolic BP <20 mm Hg and decline in diastolic BP <10 mm Hg) and a mild increase in HR (increase of <30/min). Tilt table testing can be used to evaluate patients who have syncope of unknown cause, suspected vasovagal or orthostatic syncope, and/or autonomic dysfunction, including orthostatic hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Prior to tilt table testing, patients are instructed to abstain from alcohol and caffeine for 12 hours and to fast for at least 2 hours. During testing, individuals lie horizontally on a padded table with lateral armrests that position the arms at the level of the heart. Adjustable nonconstricting straps secure the chest and legs. Patients are monitored with continuous ECG. Brachial artery systolic pressure is measured at 1-minute intervals with sphygmomanometry, and finger-cuff photoplethysmography can be used for continuous beat-to-beat BP monitoring. After the patient rests supine for at least 10 minutes, the motorized table moves into a 70° incline within 10 seconds. Throughout the test, patients report any symptoms. The duration of tilt table testing ranges from 5 to 10 minutes for patients with suspected orthostatic intolerance to 30 to 45 minutes for patients undergoing evaluation for vasovagal syncope. False-positive results occur in 10% to 15% of asymptomatic control individuals.1,2The sensitivity of tilt table testing is difficult to assess because there is no accepted criterion standard, and there may be protocol variability among centers performing this test.1-4 Tilt table testing is contraindicated in pregnant individuals and in those with severe coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease because hypotension may precipitate myocardial or cerebral ischemia. Medicare reimbursement for tilt table testing in 2023 was approximately $370.5 During tilt table testing, the patient’s BP was stable and her HR increased more than 30/min above her baseline HR during minutes 3 through 10 of testing, reaching a peak of 42/min above baseline. The hemodynamic finding of increased HR without simultaneous hypotension is characteristic of POTS, defined as chronic orthostatic intolerance for at least 3 months with a sustained HR increase of 30/min or more above baseline (40/min for patients aged 8-19 years) that occurs within 10 minutes of standing up or head-up tilt, without simultaneous hypotension.6POTS develops in approximately 1% of people after COVID-19 infection,7and in 15% to 20% of patients with post–COVID-19 condition (long COVID).8-10 Orthostatic vital signs involves measuring BP and HR after patients lie supine for at least 5 minutes, and then at 1, 3, and sometimes 5 minutes after standing. Compared to tilt table testing, active standing typically causes a greater initial transient rise in HR. The patient was treated with midodrine, 7.5 mg 3 times daily, pyridostigmine, 60 mg 3 times daily, and ivabradine, 2.5 mg twice daily. She was instructed to increase salt intake to 5 to 10 g/d, drink fluids up to 2 to 3 L/d, and wear lower extremity compressive garments. She began a progressive exercise program that included lower extremity strength training. At 3 years after COVID-19 infection, her symptoms of fatigue and palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain when standing were improved. She had returned to work part-time, could walk for 20 minutes, and exercised on a stationary bicycle for 10 minutes twice weekly.

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

4. Frustration

   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: D. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) Tilt table testing is performed in the inpatient or outpatient setting and measures an individual’s symptoms and hemodynamic response to the downward displacement of intravascular volume with movement from the supine to upright position. During tilt table testing, movement from horizontal to upright positioning normally provokes an increase in sympathetic adrenergic outflow to sustain cardiac output. A normal response is a mild decrease in BP (decline in systolic BP <20 mm Hg and decline in diastolic BP <10 mm Hg) and a mild increase in HR (increase of <30/min). Tilt table testing can be used to evaluate patients who have syncope of unknown cause, suspected vasovagal or orthostatic syncope, and/or autonomic dysfunction, including orthostatic hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Prior to tilt table testing, patients are instructed to abstain from alcohol and caffeine for 12 hours and to fast for at least 2 hours. During testing, individuals lie horizontally on a padded table with lateral armrests that position the arms at the level of the heart. Adjustable nonconstricting straps secure the chest and legs. Patients are monitored with continuous ECG. Brachial artery systolic pressure is measured at 1-minute intervals with sphygmomanometry, and finger-cuff photoplethysmography can be used for continuous beat-to-beat BP monitoring. After the patient rests supine for at least 10 minutes, the motorized table moves into a 70° incline within 10 seconds. Throughout the test, patients report any symptoms. The duration of tilt table testing ranges from 5 to 10 minutes for patients with suspected orthostatic intolerance to 30 to 45 minutes for patients undergoing evaluation for vasovagal syncope. False-positive results occur in 10% to 15% of asymptomatic control individuals.1,2The sensitivity of tilt table testing is difficult to assess because there is no accepted criterion standard, and there may be protocol variability among centers performing this test.1-4 Tilt table testing is contraindicated in pregnant individuals and in those with severe coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease because hypotension may precipitate myocardial or cerebral ischemia. Medicare reimbursement for tilt table testing in 2023 was approximately $370.5 During tilt table testing, the patient’s BP was stable and her HR increased more than 30/min above her baseline HR during minutes 3 through 10 of testing, reaching a peak of 42/min above baseline. The hemodynamic finding of increased HR without simultaneous hypotension is characteristic of POTS, defined as chronic orthostatic intolerance for at least 3 months with a sustained HR increase of 30/min or more above baseline (40/min for patients aged 8-19 years) that occurs within 10 minutes of standing up or head-up tilt, without simultaneous hypotension.6POTS develops in approximately 1% of people after COVID-19 infection,7and in 15% to 20% of patients with post–COVID-19 condition (long COVID).8-10 Orthostatic vital signs involves measuring BP and HR after patients lie supine for at least 5 minutes, and then at 1, 3, and sometimes 5 minutes after standing. Compared to tilt table testing, active standing typically causes a greater initial transient rise in HR. The patient was treated with midodrine, 7.5 mg 3 times daily, pyridostigmine, 60 mg 3 times daily, and ivabradine, 2.5 mg twice daily. She was instructed to increase salt intake to 5 to 10 g/d, drink fluids up to 2 to 3 L/d, and wear lower extremity compressive garments. She began a progressive exercise program that included lower extremity strength training. At 3 years after COVID-19 infection, her symptoms of fatigue and palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain when standing were improved. She had returned to work part-time, could walk for 20 minutes, and exercised on a stationary bicycle for 10 minutes twice weekly.

case_info.explanation: D. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) Tilt table testing is performed in the inpatient or outpatient setting and measures an individual’s symptoms and hemodynamic response to the downward displacement of intravascular volume with movement from the supine to upright position. During tilt table testing, movement from horizontal to upright positioning normally provokes an increase in sympathetic adrenergic outflow to sustain cardiac output. A normal response is a mild decrease in BP (decline in systolic BP <20 mm Hg and decline in diastolic BP <10 mm Hg) and a mild increase in HR (increase of <30/min). Tilt table testing can be used to evaluate patients who have syncope of unknown cause, suspected vasovagal or orthostatic syncope, and/or autonomic dysfunction, including orthostatic hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Prior to tilt table testing, patients are instructed to abstain from alcohol and caffeine for 12 hours and to fast for at least 2 hours. During testing, individuals lie horizontally on a padded table with lateral armrests that position the arms at the level of the heart. Adjustable nonconstricting straps secure the chest and legs. Patients are monitored with continuous ECG. Brachial artery systolic pressure is measured at 1-minute intervals with sphygmomanometry, and finger-cuff photoplethysmography can be used for continuous beat-to-beat BP monitoring. After the patient rests supine for at least 10 minutes, the motorized table moves into a 70° incline within 10 seconds. Throughout the test, patients report any symptoms. The duration of tilt table testing ranges from 5 to 10 minutes for patients with suspected orthostatic intolerance to 30 to 45 minutes for patients undergoing evaluation for vasovagal syncope. False-positive results occur in 10% to 15% of asymptomatic control individuals.1,2The sensitivity of tilt table testing is difficult to assess because there is no accepted criterion standard, and there may be protocol variability among centers performing this test.1-4 Tilt table testing is contraindicated in pregnant individuals and in those with severe coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease because hypotension may precipitate myocardial or cerebral ischemia. Medicare reimbursement for tilt table testing in 2023 was approximately $370.5 During tilt table testing, the patient’s BP was stable and her HR increased more than 30/min above her baseline HR during minutes 3 through 10 of testing, reaching a peak of 42/min above baseline. The hemodynamic finding of increased HR without simultaneous hypotension is characteristic of POTS, defined as chronic orthostatic intolerance for at least 3 months with a sustained HR increase of 30/min or more above baseline (40/min for patients aged 8-19 years) that occurs within 10 minutes of standing up or head-up tilt, without simultaneous hypotension.6POTS develops in approximately 1% of people after COVID-19 infection,7and in 15% to 20% of patients with post–COVID-19 condition (long COVID).8-10 Orthostatic vital signs involves measuring BP and HR after patients lie supine for at least 5 minutes, and then at 1, 3, and sometimes 5 minutes after standing. Compared to tilt table testing, active standing typically causes a greater initial transient rise in HR. The patient was treated with midodrine, 7.5 mg 3 times daily, pyridostigmine, 60 mg 3 times daily, and ivabradine, 2.5 mg twice daily. She was instructed to increase salt intake to 5 to 10 g/d, drink fluids up to 2 to 3 L/d, and wear lower extremity compressive garments. She began a progressive exercise program that included lower extremity strength training. At 3 years after COVID-19 infection, her symptoms of fatigue and palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain when standing were improved. She had returned to work part-time, could walk for 20 minutes, and exercised on a stationary bicycle for 10 minutes twice weekly.

case_info.explanation: D. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) Tilt table testing is performed in the inpatient or outpatient setting and measures an individual’s symptoms and hemodynamic response to the downward displacement of intravascular volume with movement from the supine to upright position. During tilt table testing, movement from horizontal to upright positioning normally provokes an increase in sympathetic adrenergic outflow to sustain cardiac output. A normal response is a mild decrease in BP (decline in systolic BP <20 mm Hg and decline in diastolic BP <10 mm Hg) and a mild increase in HR (increase of <30/min). Tilt table testing can be used to evaluate patients who have syncope of unknown cause, suspected vasovagal or orthostatic syncope, and/or autonomic dysfunction, including orthostatic hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Prior to tilt table testing, patients are instructed to abstain from alcohol and caffeine for 12 hours and to fast for at least 2 hours. During testing, individuals lie horizontally on a padded table with lateral armrests that position the arms at the level of the heart. Adjustable nonconstricting straps secure the chest and legs. Patients are monitored with continuous ECG. Brachial artery systolic pressure is measured at 1-minute intervals with sphygmomanometry, and finger-cuff photoplethysmography can be used for continuous beat-to-beat BP monitoring. After the patient rests supine for at least 10 minutes, the motorized table moves into a 70° incline within 10 seconds. Throughout the test, patients report any symptoms. The duration of tilt table testing ranges from 5 to 10 minutes for patients with suspected orthostatic intolerance to 30 to 45 minutes for patients undergoing evaluation for vasovagal syncope. False-positive results occur in 10% to 15% of asymptomatic control individuals.1,2The sensitivity of tilt table testing is difficult to assess because there is no accepted criterion standard, and there may be protocol variability among centers performing this test.1-4 Tilt table testing is contraindicated in pregnant individuals and in those with severe coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease because hypotension may precipitate myocardial or cerebral ischemia. Medicare reimbursement for tilt table testing in 2023 was approximately $370.5 During tilt table testing, the patient’s BP was stable and her HR increased more than 30/min above her baseline HR during minutes 3 through 10 of testing, reaching a peak of 42/min above baseline. The hemodynamic finding of increased HR without simultaneous hypotension is characteristic of POTS, defined as chronic orthostatic intolerance for at least 3 months with a sustained HR increase of 30/min or more above baseline (40/min for patients aged 8-19 years) that occurs within 10 minutes of standing up or head-up tilt, without simultaneous hypotension.6POTS develops in approximately 1% of people after COVID-19 infection,7and in 15% to 20% of patients with post–COVID-19 condition (long COVID).8-10 Orthostatic vital signs involves measuring BP and HR after patients lie supine for at least 5 minutes, and then at 1, 3, and sometimes 5 minutes after standing. Compared to tilt table testing, active standing typically causes a greater initial transient rise in HR. The patient was treated with midodrine, 7.5 mg 3 times daily, pyridostigmine, 60 mg 3 times daily, and ivabradine, 2.5 mg twice daily. She was instructed to increase salt intake to 5 to 10 g/d, drink fluids up to 2 to 3 L/d, and wear lower extremity compressive garments. She began a progressive exercise program that included lower extremity strength training. At 3 years after COVID-19 infection, her symptoms of fatigue and palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain when standing were improved. She had returned to work part-time, could walk for 20 minutes, and exercised on a stationary bicycle for 10 minutes twice weekly.

case_info.explanation: D. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) Tilt table testing is performed in the inpatient or outpatient setting and measures an individual’s symptoms and hemodynamic response to the downward displacement of intravascular volume with movement from the supine to upright position. During tilt table testing, movement from horizontal to upright positioning normally provokes an increase in sympathetic adrenergic outflow to sustain cardiac output. A normal response is a mild decrease in BP (decline in systolic BP <20 mm Hg and decline in diastolic BP <10 mm Hg) and a mild increase in HR (increase of <30/min). Tilt table testing can be used to evaluate patients who have syncope of unknown cause, suspected vasovagal or orthostatic syncope, and/or autonomic dysfunction, including orthostatic hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Prior to tilt table testing, patients are instructed to abstain from alcohol and caffeine for 12 hours and to fast for at least 2 hours. During testing, individuals lie horizontally on a padded table with lateral armrests that position the arms at the level of the heart. Adjustable nonconstricting straps secure the chest and legs. Patients are monitored with continuous ECG. Brachial artery systolic pressure is measured at 1-minute intervals with sphygmomanometry, and finger-cuff photoplethysmography can be used for continuous beat-to-beat BP monitoring. After the patient rests supine for at least 10 minutes, the motorized table moves into a 70° incline within 10 seconds. Throughout the test, patients report any symptoms. The duration of tilt table testing ranges from 5 to 10 minutes for patients with suspected orthostatic intolerance to 30 to 45 minutes for patients undergoing evaluation for vasovagal syncope. False-positive results occur in 10% to 15% of asymptomatic control individuals.1,2The sensitivity of tilt table testing is difficult to assess because there is no accepted criterion standard, and there may be protocol variability among centers performing this test.1-4 Tilt table testing is contraindicated in pregnant individuals and in those with severe coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease because hypotension may precipitate myocardial or cerebral ischemia. Medicare reimbursement for tilt table testing in 2023 was approximately $370.5 During tilt table testing, the patient’s BP was stable and her HR increased more than 30/min above her baseline HR during minutes 3 through 10 of testing, reaching a peak of 42/min above baseline. The hemodynamic finding of increased HR without simultaneous hypotension is characteristic of POTS, defined as chronic orthostatic intolerance for at least 3 months with a sustained HR increase of 30/min or more above baseline (40/min for patients aged 8-19 years) that occurs within 10 minutes of standing up or head-up tilt, without simultaneous hypotension.6POTS develops in approximately 1% of people after COVID-19 infection,7and in 15% to 20% of patients with post–COVID-19 condition (long COVID).8-10 Orthostatic vital signs involves measuring BP and HR after patients lie supine for at least 5 minutes, and then at 1, 3, and sometimes 5 minutes after standing. Compared to tilt table testing, active standing typically causes a greater initial transient rise in HR. The patient was treated with midodrine, 7.5 mg 3 times daily, pyridostigmine, 60 mg 3 times daily, and ivabradine, 2.5 mg twice daily. She was instructed to increase salt intake to 5 to 10 g/d, drink fluids up to 2 to 3 L/d, and wear lower extremity compressive garments. She began a progressive exercise program that included lower extremity strength training. At 3 years after COVID-19 infection, her symptoms of fatigue and palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain when standing were improved. She had returned to work part-time, could walk for 20 minutes, and exercised on a stationary bicycle for 10 minutes twice weekly.

case_info.explanation: D. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) Tilt table testing is performed in the inpatient or outpatient setting and measures an individual’s symptoms and hemodynamic response to the downward displacement of intravascular volume with movement from the supine to upright position. During tilt table testing, movement from horizontal to upright positioning normally provokes an increase in sympathetic adrenergic outflow to sustain cardiac output. A normal response is a mild decrease in BP (decline in systolic BP <20 mm Hg and decline in diastolic BP <10 mm Hg) and a mild increase in HR (increase of <30/min). Tilt table testing can be used to evaluate patients who have syncope of unknown cause, suspected vasovagal or orthostatic syncope, and/or autonomic dysfunction, including orthostatic hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Prior to tilt table testing, patients are instructed to abstain from alcohol and caffeine for 12 hours and to fast for at least 2 hours. During testing, individuals lie horizontally on a padded table with lateral armrests that position the arms at the level of the heart. Adjustable nonconstricting straps secure the chest and legs. Patients are monitored with continuous ECG. Brachial artery systolic pressure is measured at 1-minute intervals with sphygmomanometry, and finger-cuff photoplethysmography can be used for continuous beat-to-beat BP monitoring. After the patient rests supine for at least 10 minutes, the motorized table moves into a 70° incline within 10 seconds. Throughout the test, patients report any symptoms. The duration of tilt table testing ranges from 5 to 10 minutes for patients with suspected orthostatic intolerance to 30 to 45 minutes for patients undergoing evaluation for vasovagal syncope. False-positive results occur in 10% to 15% of asymptomatic control individuals.1,2The sensitivity of tilt table testing is difficult to assess because there is no accepted criterion standard, and there may be protocol variability among centers performing this test.1-4 Tilt table testing is contraindicated in pregnant individuals and in those with severe coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease because hypotension may precipitate myocardial or cerebral ischemia. Medicare reimbursement for tilt table testing in 2023 was approximately $370.5 During tilt table testing, the patient’s BP was stable and her HR increased more than 30/min above her baseline HR during minutes 3 through 10 of testing, reaching a peak of 42/min above baseline. The hemodynamic finding of increased HR without simultaneous hypotension is characteristic of POTS, defined as chronic orthostatic intolerance for at least 3 months with a sustained HR increase of 30/min or more above baseline (40/min for patients aged 8-19 years) that occurs within 10 minutes of standing up or head-up tilt, without simultaneous hypotension.6POTS develops in approximately 1% of people after COVID-19 infection,7and in 15% to 20% of patients with post–COVID-19 condition (long COVID).8-10 Orthostatic vital signs involves measuring BP and HR after patients lie supine for at least 5 minutes, and then at 1, 3, and sometimes 5 minutes after standing. Compared to tilt table testing, active standing typically causes a greater initial transient rise in HR. The patient was treated with midodrine, 7.5 mg 3 times daily, pyridostigmine, 60 mg 3 times daily, and ivabradine, 2.5 mg twice daily. She was instructed to increase salt intake to 5 to 10 g/d, drink fluids up to 2 to 3 L/d, and wear lower extremity compressive garments. She began a progressive exercise program that included lower extremity strength training. At 3 years after COVID-19 infection, her symptoms of fatigue and palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain when standing were improved. She had returned to work part-time, could walk for 20 minutes, and exercised on a stationary bicycle for 10 minutes twice weekly.

case_info.explanation: D. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) Tilt table testing is performed in the inpatient or outpatient setting and measures an individual’s symptoms and hemodynamic response to the downward displacement of intravascular volume with movement from the supine to upright position. During tilt table testing, movement from horizontal to upright positioning normally provokes an increase in sympathetic adrenergic outflow to sustain cardiac output. A normal response is a mild decrease in BP (decline in systolic BP <20 mm Hg and decline in diastolic BP <10 mm Hg) and a mild increase in HR (increase of <30/min). Tilt table testing can be used to evaluate patients who have syncope of unknown cause, suspected vasovagal or orthostatic syncope, and/or autonomic dysfunction, including orthostatic hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Prior to tilt table testing, patients are instructed to abstain from alcohol and caffeine for 12 hours and to fast for at least 2 hours. During testing, individuals lie horizontally on a padded table with lateral armrests that position the arms at the level of the heart. Adjustable nonconstricting straps secure the chest and legs. Patients are monitored with continuous ECG. Brachial artery systolic pressure is measured at 1-minute intervals with sphygmomanometry, and finger-cuff photoplethysmography can be used for continuous beat-to-beat BP monitoring. After the patient rests supine for at least 10 minutes, the motorized table moves into a 70° incline within 10 seconds. Throughout the test, patients report any symptoms. The duration of tilt table testing ranges from 5 to 10 minutes for patients with suspected orthostatic intolerance to 30 to 45 minutes for patients undergoing evaluation for vasovagal syncope. False-positive results occur in 10% to 15% of asymptomatic control individuals.1,2The sensitivity of tilt table testing is difficult to assess because there is no accepted criterion standard, and there may be protocol variability among centers performing this test.1-4 Tilt table testing is contraindicated in pregnant individuals and in those with severe coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease because hypotension may precipitate myocardial or cerebral ischemia. Medicare reimbursement for tilt table testing in 2023 was approximately $370.5 During tilt table testing, the patient’s BP was stable and her HR increased more than 30/min above her baseline HR during minutes 3 through 10 of testing, reaching a peak of 42/min above baseline. The hemodynamic finding of increased HR without simultaneous hypotension is characteristic of POTS, defined as chronic orthostatic intolerance for at least 3 months with a sustained HR increase of 30/min or more above baseline (40/min for patients aged 8-19 years) that occurs within 10 minutes of standing up or head-up tilt, without simultaneous hypotension.6POTS develops in approximately 1% of people after COVID-19 infection,7and in 15% to 20% of patients with post–COVID-19 condition (long COVID).8-10 Orthostatic vital signs involves measuring BP and HR after patients lie supine for at least 5 minutes, and then at 1, 3, and sometimes 5 minutes after standing. Compared to tilt table testing, active standing typically causes a greater initial transient rise in HR. The patient was treated with midodrine, 7.5 mg 3 times daily, pyridostigmine, 60 mg 3 times daily, and ivabradine, 2.5 mg twice daily. She was instructed to increase salt intake to 5 to 10 g/d, drink fluids up to 2 to 3 L/d, and wear lower extremity compressive garments. She began a progressive exercise program that included lower extremity strength training. At 3 years after COVID-19 infection, her symptoms of fatigue and palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain when standing were improved. She had returned to work part-time, could walk for 20 minutes, and exercised on a stationary bicycle for 10 minutes twice weekly.

case_info.explanation: D. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) Tilt table testing is performed in the inpatient or outpatient setting and measures an individual’s symptoms and hemodynamic response to the downward displacement of intravascular volume with movement from the supine to upright position. During tilt table testing, movement from horizontal to upright positioning normally provokes an increase in sympathetic adrenergic outflow to sustain cardiac output. A normal response is a mild decrease in BP (decline in systolic BP <20 mm Hg and decline in diastolic BP <10 mm Hg) and a mild increase in HR (increase of <30/min). Tilt table testing can be used to evaluate patients who have syncope of unknown cause, suspected vasovagal or orthostatic syncope, and/or autonomic dysfunction, including orthostatic hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Prior to tilt table testing, patients are instructed to abstain from alcohol and caffeine for 12 hours and to fast for at least 2 hours. During testing, individuals lie horizontally on a padded table with lateral armrests that position the arms at the level of the heart. Adjustable nonconstricting straps secure the chest and legs. Patients are monitored with continuous ECG. Brachial artery systolic pressure is measured at 1-minute intervals with sphygmomanometry, and finger-cuff photoplethysmography can be used for continuous beat-to-beat BP monitoring. After the patient rests supine for at least 10 minutes, the motorized table moves into a 70° incline within 10 seconds. Throughout the test, patients report any symptoms. The duration of tilt table testing ranges from 5 to 10 minutes for patients with suspected orthostatic intolerance to 30 to 45 minutes for patients undergoing evaluation for vasovagal syncope. False-positive results occur in 10% to 15% of asymptomatic control individuals.1,2The sensitivity of tilt table testing is difficult to assess because there is no accepted criterion standard, and there may be protocol variability among centers performing this test.1-4 Tilt table testing is contraindicated in pregnant individuals and in those with severe coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease because hypotension may precipitate myocardial or cerebral ischemia. Medicare reimbursement for tilt table testing in 2023 was approximately $370.5 During tilt table testing, the patient’s BP was stable and her HR increased more than 30/min above her baseline HR during minutes 3 through 10 of testing, reaching a peak of 42/min above baseline. The hemodynamic finding of increased HR without simultaneous hypotension is characteristic of POTS, defined as chronic orthostatic intolerance for at least 3 months with a sustained HR increase of 30/min or more above baseline (40/min for patients aged 8-19 years) that occurs within 10 minutes of standing up or head-up tilt, without simultaneous hypotension.6POTS develops in approximately 1% of people after COVID-19 infection,7and in 15% to 20% of patients with post–COVID-19 condition (long COVID).8-10 Orthostatic vital signs involves measuring BP and HR after patients lie supine for at least 5 minutes, and then at 1, 3, and sometimes 5 minutes after standing. Compared to tilt table testing, active standing typically causes a greater initial transient rise in HR. The patient was treated with midodrine, 7.5 mg 3 times daily, pyridostigmine, 60 mg 3 times daily, and ivabradine, 2.5 mg twice daily. She was instructed to increase salt intake to 5 to 10 g/d, drink fluids up to 2 to 3 L/d, and wear lower extremity compressive garments. She began a progressive exercise program that included lower extremity strength training. At 3 years after COVID-19 infection, her symptoms of fatigue and palpitations, dyspnea, and chest pain when standing were improved.
